hints: Picture each halogen in the lab at 293 K and recall how the colour gets darker and deeper as you go down Group 17 from pale green-yellow toward brown and then to almost black solid.
walkthrough:
Link colour to position in the group**
Think of the three halogens side by side. Chlorine at the top is a very pale green gas, bromine in the middle is a brown liquid that gives off brown vapour, and iodine at the bottom is a dark grey or almost black solid. The colour deepens down the group.
Final answer: chlorine: green; bromine: brown; iodine: (dark) grey

hints: Recall the physical states of chlorine, bromine and iodine at room temperature to deduce whether boiling point increases or decreases.
Identify the specific type of intermolecular force operating between simple diatomic halogen molecules.
Consider how the total number of electrons in the molecule changes down Group 17 and how this affects the strength of temporary dipoles.
walkthrough:
Clarify volatility in everyday terms**
Do not let the word volatility confuse you. It simply means how easily a substance turns into a gas. Picture the halogens at room temperature: chlorine is a gas, bromine is a liquid, and iodine is a solid. That tells you straight away that boiling points rise down the group, so volatility decreases.

Identify what is actually breaking**
When liquid bromine boils, are you snapping the $\text{Br-Br}$ covalent bonds? Never. Halogens are simple molecular substances. The covalent bonds inside each $\text{X}_2$ molecule stay completely intact. All you are doing is separating one molecule from its neighbour, so the only attractions to overcome are the weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces between molecules.

Track why the forces strengthen down the group**
Look at the electrons. A $\text{Cl}_2$ molecule has 34 electrons, $\text{Br}_2$ has 70 and $\text{I}_2$ has 106. With a much larger electron cloud, the electrons can shift and distort much more easily. This greater polarisability sets up stronger temporary dipoles, producing significantly stronger instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces.

Connect the forces back to energy**
Stronger attractions between molecules need more thermal energy to pull apart. Because it takes more heat to separate $\text{I}_2$ molecules than $\text{Cl}_2$ molecules, boiling point increases and volatility decreases down the group.

Final answer: Volatility decreases down Group 17 from chlorine to iodine.
Down the group, the number of electrons per molecule increases, resulting in stronger instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces between molecules.
More thermal energy is required to overcome these stronger intermolecular forces.

hints: Think about which halogen is more reactive and displaces the other from solution, then remove the $\text{Na}^+$ spectator ions and balance atoms and charge.
walkthrough:
Spot the displacement pattern**
Bromine is above iodine in Group 17, so it is the more powerful oxidising agent. That means $\text{Br}_2$ will displace $\text{I}_2$ from $\text{NaI}$ solution. Sodium ions, $\text{Na}^+$, do nothing and are omitted from the ionic equation.

Balance atoms and charge**
You need two $\text{I}^-$ ions to supply two iodine atoms for $\text{I}_2$, and this also balances the charge: $2-$ on each side. So the balanced ionic equation is $$\text{Br}_2 + 2\text{I}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Br}^- + \text{I}_2$$

hints: Follow the electrons in your equation from (c)(i) and check which species gains electrons while the oxidation number of the other species increases.
walkthrough:
Use electron gain and loss to decide the role**
Look closely at your ionic equation. Each $\text{I}^-$ loses one electron to form $\text{I}_2$: $$2\text{I}^- \rightarrow \text{I}_2 + 2e^-$$ Those electrons are gained by $\text{Br}_2$ to form $2\text{Br}^-$. A species that causes oxidation by taking electrons while itself being reduced is an oxidising agent. Here $\text{Br}_2$ oxidises $\text{I}^-$, with iodine changing in oxidation number from -1 to 0, so bromine is the oxidising agent.
Final answer: Bromine is an oxidising agent as it removes electrons from $\text{I}^-$ / the oxidation number of $\text{I}^-$ increases from -1 to 0.

hints: Treat this first step as a simple proton transfer from concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to $\text{Br}^-$, forming $\text{HBr}$ and a hydrogensulfate salt, without any change in oxidation number.
walkthrough:
See it as proton donation only**
At first, concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ simply acts as an acid. It donates a proton, $\text{H}^+$, to $\text{Br}^-$ to make $\text{HBr}$. No oxidation numbers change here, so this is acid-base chemistry, not redox. The other product is sodium hydrogensulfate: $$\text{NaBr} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{HBr} + \text{NaHSO}_4$$

hints: Recall that all three sodium halides first make their hydrogen halide, but some hydrogen halides are then destroyed by further reaction with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.
Think about how reducing power of $\text{Cl}^-$, $\text{Br}^-$ and $\text{I}^-$ changes down Group 17.
Connect the strength as a reducing agent to whether the halide ion can reduce the sulfur in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, and decide which hydrogen halide survives in the highest yield.
walkthrough:
Separate the two stages of the reaction**
Keep the picture clear in your mind. Stage 1 happens for all three salts: $$\text{NaX} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{HX} + \text{NaHSO}_4$$ Stage 2 is the problem. Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is also a strong oxidising agent and can oxidise the $\text{HX}$ just made, reducing sulfur from +6 to +4, 0 or -2. If Stage 2 happens, the yield of $\text{HX}$ falls.

Compare reducing power down the group**
Reducing power means willingness to lose electrons. Down Group 17 the halide ions get larger, the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are lost more easily. Reducing strength therefore increases: $\text{Cl}^- < \text{Br}^- < \text{I}^-$.

Decide which hydrogen halide survives**
$\text{Cl}^-$ is too weak a reducing agent to reduce $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, so $\text{HCl}$ is not destroyed and $\text{NaCl}$ gives the largest percentage yield. In contrast, $\text{Br}^-$ and $\text{I}^-$ are strong enough to reduce $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ further, for example $\text{HBr}$ is oxidised to $\text{Br}_2$ and $\text{HI}$ is oxidised to $\text{I}_2$, so much less $\text{HBr}$ and $\text{HI}$ remains.

Final answer: identity of sodium halide: sodium chloride, $\text{NaCl}$
$\text{Cl}^-$ is not a strong enough reducing agent to reduce $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.
$\text{Br}^-$ and $\text{I}^-$ are strong enough reducing agents to react further with the S in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, destroying some $\text{HBr}$ and $\text{HI}$ formed.
